newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council presses for Angola unity government.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council presses for Angola unity government.

text.p: The Security Council issued a statement on Friday aimed at strengthening the hand of Secretary-General Kofi Annan when he arrives in Angola on Saturday to try to speed the establishment of a long-delayed national unity government.

The statement, read at a brief meeting, repeated a threat made last month that the council was prepared to consider sanctions against the party responsible for any further postponement. A report by Annan this week mainly blamed the former UNITA rebel movement for the delays.

Establishment of a national unity government, originally scheduled for Jan. 25, would mark the culmination of a 1994 accord ending years of civil war signed in Lusaka, Zambia, by the government of President Jose Eduardo dos Santos and UNITA -- the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola.

The statement said the council "once again expresses its deep concern that the government of unity and national reconciliation (GURN) has not yet been established, owing primarily to the failure of UNITA to send all of its officials to Luanda as previous agreed."

The council expressed its "full support for the secretary-general in his mission to Angola to assess the situation and impress upon the parties the need to establish the GURN without any further delay."
"It calls upon the parties, in particular UNITA, to cooperate fully with the secretary-general ... and to use the occasion of the secretary-general's visit to install the GURN."

The council said it would "consider the imposition of measures" including those mentioned in a September 1993 resolution "against the party responsible for the failure to form the GURN." That resolution threatened UNITA with trade and travel restrictions because of delays in peace efforts and the absence of a ceasefire.

The council said that, after Annan's next report, it would consider the role of the United Nations in Angola after the March 31 expiration of the mandate of a 6,600-strong force, called the U.N. Angola Verification Mission (UNAVEM III), which has been helping implement the peace process.
After UNAVEM ends its mandate and completes its withdrawal over several months, it is expected to be succeeded by a smaller U.N. observer mission that would remain at least until the end of the year.
